notes:
Below are my notes on Titus 3. I ran out of research steps before reaching several sources, so some verses are covered only lightly. Those gaps are listed at the end.

---

**v. 1**
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** In Greek, "remind" is in the present tense, so it means "keep on reminding." Because Cretans had a reputation for being difficult (Titus 1:12), the command to obey rulers had special meaning. "Ready for every good work" keeps submission from turning into a passive faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/
- **Historical background (Bible Hub commentaries):** At the time, Crete had been under Roman rule for roughly 125 years. Historians like Polybius dwelt on the turbulent and factious spirit of its people, and Jewish Christians there may also have resented Rome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-1.htm
- **Benson:** Benson thinks Judaizing teachers in Crete may have been saying that no obedience was due from the worshippers of the true God to magistrates who were idolaters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-1.htm
- **Meyer** disagrees with tying the command to Cretan character. He points out that similar commands appear in other letters, and that Christians needed the reminder anyway all the more that the authorities were heathen. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-1.htm
- **Limits on obedience:** Barnes says Christians obey rulers only in what is not contrary to the word of God (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bis/titus/3-1.html). Coffman also makes an exception where obeying would mean disobeying God (Acts 5:29) (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-1.html). Precept Austin says the same (https://www.preceptaustin.org/titus_31-8).

**v. 2**
- **Guzik:** This is a distinctly Christian kindness. It does not come from good manners but from knowing who we are, and who others are, in Jesus' heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/
- **Constable:** The word translated "peaceable" (Greek *amachous*) literally means non-fighting. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-1.html
- **Precept Austin:** There were good reasons to criticise the people who lived in and ruled Crete, but Paul told Christians not to slander them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/titus_31-8

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** This verse explains why the reminders in vv. 1–2 matter. Remembering our past builds four things: gratitude, humility, kindness toward people still in that condition, and faith that God can change them. He quotes White: "We ourselves are a living proof of the power of God's grace." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/

**v. 4**
- **Guzik:** We did not rescue ourselves. God reached out to us long before we reached out to Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/
- **Piper (Desiring God):** God is called "our Savior" in v. 4 and Jesus is called "our Savior" in v. 6. Piper treats Jesus as the appearing of God's kindness. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/through-the-washing-of-regeneration
- **Precept Austin:** The verse clearly underscores Paul's belief in the deity of Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/titus_37-8

**v. 5 (the main dividing verse: does "washing of regeneration" mean baptism?)**
- **Common ground:** Works are not the basis of salvation. Matthew Henry puts it this way: works must be in the saved, but are not among the causes of their salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-5.htm
- **Baptist:**
  - Gill says the washing is *not* water baptism. The Spirit is the cause of regeneration and the Word is the means. People should be regenerated before they are baptized, and some, like Simon Magus, are baptized without being regenerated. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/titus/3-5.html
  - Piper says the washing is not baptism, because new birth comes from God's free mercy, Not baptism. Not any works done by us in righteousness. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/through-the-washing-of-regeneration
  - Wiersbe and Hiebert (quoted by Precept Austin and Guzik) see an inner washing that is publicly confessed in baptism. https://www.preceptaustin.org/titus_34-8
- **Charismatic/Calvary (Guzik):** The only other New Testament use of the Greek word for "washing" is Ephesians 5:26, which is about cleansing by the Word. Guzik says baptism does not save. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/
- **Reformed:**
  - Calvin agrees the verse alludes to baptism. Salvation is not contained in the water, but God inwardly accomplishes by his power what he exhibits by the outward sign. In believers baptism is always effective.
  - Matthew Henry calls baptism the outward sign and seal of an inward work.
  - Both: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-5.html
- **Methodist:** Adam Clarke says Paul means baptism as a *visible sign*. He also writes that Baptism changes nothing; the grace signified by it cleanses and purifies. They who think baptism to be regeneration, neither know the Scriptures nor the power of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-5.html
- **Presbyterian (Barnes):** Baptism is the emblem of regeneration, not its means. Barnes thinks Paul added "renewing of the Holy Ghost" so that no one would assume baptism is all the regeneration needed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-5.html
- **Anglican-leaning (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Bible Hub):** The "laver" is the baptismal font, *designed to be the visible instrument of regeneration*. The commentary cites the Church of England's Article XXVII and says infants are "charitably presumed" to be regenerated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-5.htm
- **Lutheran:**
  - Luther (described in a Gospel Coalition article) taught that baptismal water receives power through the Word to become the "washing of regeneration," and that the baptized infant is regenerated and given faith. The article's author is a critic of Luther's view on this point. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/sola-fide-compromised-martin-luther-and-the-doctrine-of-baptism/
  - The ISBE's entry on Lutheran doctrine says baptism is called the "washing of regeneration" not merely because it symbolizes it, or pledges a man to it, but also, and chiefly, because it effects it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/search/dictionary/viewTopic.cfm?topic=IT0001147
- **Churches of Christ (Coffman; "Contending for the Faith"):** The washing is without a doubt, baptism, which these commentators link with Mark 16:16. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-5.html
- **Greek grammar:** Vincent says the phrase "distinctly refers to baptism" but has no regenerating effect without faith. Commentators disagree about whether "renewing" also depends on "washing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-5.htm
- **Catholic:** Catholic.com says the "washing of regeneration" is baptism and that It actually does something to us. It regenerates, says Scripture. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/symbolic-baptism-just-wont-wash. Another article calls baptism an instrument of salvation instituted by Christ. https://www.catholic.com/qa/how-baptism-saves-us
- **"Regeneration":** The same Greek word appears in Matthew 19:28, where it means the renewal of all things. Piper says our new birth is the firstfruits of that coming renewal. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/through-the-washing-of-regeneration

**v. 6**
- **Matthew Henry:** God gives the Spirit not with a scanty and niggardly hand, but most freely and plentifully. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-7.html
- **Constable:** The outpouring happened first at Pentecost and happens again whenever someone is converted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-7.html
- **Trapp:** The Spirit is poured out "as it were by pail fulls," linking the verse to Joel 2:28. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/tit-3.cfm
- **Ligonier:** We live in the age the prophets longed for, when all believers enjoy the Spirit abundantly. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/justifying-grace
- **Arminian/non-denominational (Light of Israel):** This commentary pushes back on Christians who think the filling of the Spirit was only for the first century. It says the verse shows the Spirit is poured out richly now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-7.html

**v. 7**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The verse shows that God's mercy came first and provided the justification, rather than human righteousness causing God's mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-7.htm
- **Meyer:** "Justified" means "acquitted of the guilt, and with it, of the punishment." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-7.htm
- **Different views of justification:**
  - Matthew Henry (Reformed): justification is free forgiveness and being accepted through Christ's righteousness received by faith. Good works are its fruit, not its ground. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-7.html
  - Gill (Baptist): this is a *declarative* justification tied to an eternal act of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-7.htm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown combines being counted righteous with being made righteous by the Spirit's daily renewing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-7.htm
  - Coffman (Churches of Christ) sees baptism as the means God uses to bring about justification. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-7.html
- **"Hope":** Precept Austin says the word expresses certainty, not uncertainty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/titus_37-8. Clarke says the hope includes the resurrection of the body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-7.html

**v. 8**
- **Guzik:** We are saved *for* good works. The theology of Christianity is based on grace; the ethics of Christianity are based on gratitude. He also writes that faith alone saves, but saving faith is never alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/

**v. 9**
- **Guzik:** These are the same kinds of teaching Paul warned against in Titus 1:11. Guthrie notes that "avoid" literally means to turn around and face the other way. Barclay comments that discussing theology is easier than being kind at home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/
- **Poole:** Poole links the "heretic" of v. 10 to these disputes over fine points and genealogies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-10.htm

**v. 10**
- **Meaning of the word:** It is the root of "heretic." In this passage it mainly means a factious person who causes divisions, not just someone with different opinions. That is Barnes's reading, and the Revised Version margin translates it "factious." William Kelly says a "heretic" in Scripture might be sound enough in doctrine. Sources: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-10.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-10.html
- **Calvin** disagrees in part. He thinks Paul ignores the usual distinction between heretic and schismatic and includes everyone who refuses sound doctrine. He says the admonitions should be given publicly by ministers. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol43/htm/v.v.iv.htm
- **What "reject" means:**
  - Formal expulsion: Gill reads it as removal from church communion after two public warnings (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-10.html). The Pulpit Commentary reports that Vitringa understood it as excommunication.
  - Simply avoiding the person: Poole doubts the verse can support excommunication, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it means "have nothing more to do with him." Both are on https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-10.htm
- **No force allowed:** Clarke says God's only permission is to shun such a person, not to "burn him alive" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/). Barnes says the verse gives no power to torture him on the rack, or with thumb-screws, or to bind him to the stake (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-10.htm).
- **Two warnings first:** Barnes connects this to Matthew 18:15–17. The point is not to act hastily. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/3-10.htm

**v. 11**
- **Calvin:** People who will not listen to warnings are condemned by their own conscience. They sin wilfully, so more warning does no good. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol43/htm/v.v.iv.htm
- **Kelly:** The whole root of it is self. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/titus/3-10.html

**vv. 12–13**
- **Guzik:** These personal names show that Paul was a real man with real friends. White suggests Artemas or Tychicus would take Titus's place in Crete. Morgan sees "lack nothing" as showing the church's duty to support those in ministry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Paul did the same thing in Ephesus, sending Tychicus to replace Timothy. He would not leave the elders without someone carrying his delegated authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/titus-3.html

**v. 14**
- **Guzik:** Being unfruitful is a recurring concern in Titus. Paul worried about Christians who are barren yet confident in their standing with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/

**v. 15**
- **Guzik, quoting Morgan:** The closing blessing of grace matches the opening greeting, but now it includes everyone Titus served. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-3/

---

**Not covered:**
- **Modern scholarship:** I didn't get to netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes.
- **Orthodox views:** I didn't reach oca.org.
- **Lutheran sites:** I didn't read lcms.org or 1517.org directly. The Lutheran view above comes from other sites.
- **Wesley's own notes:** I didn't read these. The Methodist view comes from Clarke and Benson.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **Thin verses:** vv. 3, 4, 8 and 14 have only one or two sources each.
